$comment:
Data the two PORTABILITY rules in scripts/validate_plugin.py read: command portability (_check_command_portability) and encoding (_check_encoding). The file was named command-portability.json when only the first rule existed; it is portability.json now because both rules read ONE `exclusions` array through ONE predicate (_excluded). Two rules that both ask "is this path karta-owned?" must never be able to give two answers -- a second, parallel exclusion list is how this binder's earlier items produced the same defect twice. Rule-specific data stays in its own key; scope is shared.

COMMAND PORTABILITY: karta launched every Codex guard through `sh -c`, which a stock Windows install does not have, so every guard failed at the launcher while the guards themselves were fine. `env`, `xargs`, `grep` and `test` were measured absent from PowerShell 7 on the Windows host this rule was written for; they exist there only inside Git Bash. The rest are their common companions, listed so they cannot pass by omission. `git` is deliberately absent -- it is a real executable on every platform karta supports.

ENCODING: the same class one layer down. A text boundary with no encoding= decodes with the LOCALE codec -- cp1252 on a stock Windows checkout -- and karta's scripts read Markdown and JSON full of em dashes. These lists are committed as data rather than written into the rules so that widening either one is a reviewable diff to this file, and so a fixture can prove the rules read them.

exclusions.reason: Tracked binders are immutable: hooks/scripts/guard_binder_immutability.py denies every write to one, archived binders included. Several archived binders record `sh -c` and `python3` inside their oracle `command` strings as historical fact. A rule reaching them could never be satisfied and would wedge every future commit.

The benchmark harness measures karta from outside and ships in neither plugin projection, so a POSIX assumption there cannot reach an install — the defect class this rule exists for. Its shell dependency is also its subject: benchmarks/fixtures/shellenv.py exists to locate and drive bash portably, and benchmarks/flow fixtures are .sh scripts by design.

Generated projection of skills/, kept byte-identical by scripts/sync_codex_skills.py and guarded by its --check. Scanning it would report every finding a second time under a mirrored path. It also carries externally managed skills locked in skills-lock.json, which karta does not own.

Generated marketplace-install projection of skills/ and .codex-plugin/, kept in sync by scripts/sync_codex_skills.py and guarded by its --check. Scanning it would report every finding a second time under a mirrored path.

Externally managed skills, not karta's. Every directory under it has a complete skills-lock.json entry (AGENTS.md, 'Externally managed cross-runtime skills'), so karta neither authors nor may rewrite the code there; a finding against it names a defect no karta commit can fix. The same reasoning already excludes the .agents/skills/ copy of the same skills -- listing that mirror while scanning this one would have been the two-answers bug this file exists to prevent.

The third committed copy of the same externally managed, skills-lock.json governed skills, for the pi runtime. Excluded for the identical reason as .claude/skills/ and .agents/skills/: karta does not own the code, so it cannot repair a finding raised against it.

stdlib_loader_call_sites.$comment: The NAMED LIMITATION, bounded and made visible rather than pretended away. The encoding rule inspects CALL SITES, so a stdlib loader that opens text internally without an encoding does not fire it. This is the committed inventory of every karta-owned call site into such a loader; scripts/validate_plugin.py fails when the tree and this inventory disagree in either direction, so a new one cannot enter unnoticed and a repaired one cannot linger. `sites` entries are "<path>:<call>".
